blocks.content: This is the compact, single reference version of the entire Operating Systems course, one core fact pulled from every major module, organized for a fast final review right before an interview or exam rather than for first time learning. Every line here assumes the full concept has already been learned properly in its own dedicated chapter.

Treat this chapter as a map, not a textbook. If any single line here does not immediately make sense with a concrete example attached to it in your own head, that is the exact signal to go back to the full chapter it summarizes.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409395293-928178321.png
1. Fundamentals

{"headers":["Concept","Core fact"],"rows":[["Operating system","The software layer managing hardware and providing a consistent interface to programs above it"],["Kernel mode vs user mode","Kernel mode has full hardware access; user mode is restricted and must request privileged operations through system calls"],["System call","The controlled entry point a user program uses to request a kernel level operation"]]}
2. Processes and Threads
A process is a program in execution, with its own address space made of a code segment, a heap that grows upward as memory is allocated, and a stack that grows downward as functions are called.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409395293-446909750.png

{"headers":["Concept","Core fact"],"rows":[["Process vs thread","A process has an isolated address space; a thread shares its address space with sibling threads in the same process"],["PCB","The kernel data structure holding everything needed to describe and resume a process"],["Context switch","Saving one process or thread state and loading another; not free, it has real overhead"]]}
3. CPU Scheduling
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409396017-715452094.png

{"headers":["Algorithm","One line summary"],"rows":[["FCFS","Runs jobs in arrival order; simple but can suffer the convoy effect"],["SJF / SRTF","Runs the shortest job first; optimal average wait, but needs burst time predicted in advance"],["Priority scheduling","Runs the highest priority job first; needs aging to prevent starvation"],["Round robin","Time slices fairly across all ready processes; prevents starvation by design"]]}
4. Synchronization
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409396018-945621635.png

{"headers":["Primitive","One line summary"],"rows":[["Race condition","The bug that happens when unsynchronized concurrent access to shared data produces a wrong result"],["Mutex","A binary lock; only the thread that acquired it may release it"],["Semaphore","A counter based signal; any thread can signal it, not only the one that waited"],["Monitor","A mutex bundled with condition variables into one higher level, language supported construct"]]}
5. Deadlocks
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409396018-938230956.png

{"headers":["Concept","Core fact"],"rows":[["Deadlock","A set of processes each waiting on a resource held by another in the same set, forever, with none able to proceed"],["Four necessary conditions","Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait, all required simultaneously"],["Banker algorithm","Grants a resource request only if the resulting state is still provably safe"]]}
6. Memory Management
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409396019-865327582.png

{"headers":["Concept","Core fact"],"rows":[["Paging","Divides memory into fixed size pages and frames, translated by the page table"],["TLB","A small, fast cache of recent page table translations, avoiding a full page table walk on every access"],["Demand paging","Loads a page into RAM only the first time it is actually accessed, not all at once at startup"],["Thrashing","When a system spends more time paging than doing useful work, CPU utilization paradoxically drops"]]}
7. File Systems and Storage
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409396019-386497654.png

{"headers":["Concept","Core fact"],"rows":[["Inode","Holds a file entire metadata and data block pointers, but never its name, naming lives only in directory entries"],["Hard link vs symbolic link","A hard link is another name for the same inode; a symbolic link stores a path string and can go dangling"],["Journaling","Writes intent to a log before applying real changes, enabling fast, safe crash recovery"],["RAID","Combines multiple drives for redundancy, performance, or both; never a substitute for real backups"]]}
8. Linux and Interview Prep
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409396019-110881881.png

{"headers":["Concept","Core fact"],"rows":[["fork then exec","fork copies the current process; exec then replaces that copy program image entirely, same PID throughout"],["Zombie vs orphan","A zombie has finished but is not yet collected; an orphan is still running but has lost its parent"],["SIGKILL","Cannot be caught, blocked, or ignored under any circumstances, a guaranteed, forced termination"],["Pipe vs shared memory","A pipe copies data through the kernel and self synchronizes; shared memory needs no copying but no built in synchronization either"]]}
9. How to Use This Cheat Sheet
blocks.text: 9. How to Use This Cheat Sheet

blocks.content: Read straight through this chapter in under ten minutes as a final pass before an interview, treating any line that does not immediately trigger a clear mental example as a flag to revisit that specific full chapter one more time.

blocks.title: The honest limit of a cheat sheet
blocks.content: Nothing here replaces actually understanding why each mechanism exists and what specific problem it solves. This chapter is deliberately compressed for fast recall right before it matters, not for building the understanding in the first place.

blocks.title: One closing thought
blocks.content: Every single line in this cheat sheet traces back to a real, concrete engineering problem, not an arbitrary rule to memorize, a process needs isolation, so it gets its own address space, shared data needs protection, so mutexes exist, a crash can corrupt structures mid write, so journaling exists. Understanding the problem behind each mechanism is what actually makes it stick.

This closes the entire Operating Systems course. From what a process is, all the way through scheduling, synchronization, deadlocks, memory management, file systems, and the Linux mechanisms that implement all of it in practice, every concept in this cheat sheet connects back to a full, dedicated chapter earlier in this course.
